questions.q: What is "GPU starvation" in the context of a large training run?
options: A GPU overheating and throttling its clock speed
GPUs sitting idle because the data loader can't produce the next batch in time
A node running out of GPU memory mid-step
The scheduler refusing to allocate any GPUs to a job
questions.explain: GPU starvation is GPUs waiting on data rather than computing — the job keeps running and printing loss, just slower than the hardware allows, which makes it easy to miss.

questions.q: Why does a data loading throughput requirement depend on batch size and step time?
options: It doesn't — any DataLoader configuration works at any scale
Because each node must read and prepare its share of the global batch within the measured step time, every step
Because step time is set by the network, not the data loader
Because batch size only affects GPU memory, not throughput
questions.explain: The required throughput is derived directly from how much data a step needs and how long the step is allowed to take — it's a hard constraint, not a tuning afterthought.

questions.q: What does setting `pin_memory=True` on a PyTorch DataLoader actually do?
options: It locks the dataset file so other processes can't modify it
It allocates batches in page-locked host memory, enabling a faster, asynchronous host-to-device copy
It keeps worker processes alive across epochs
It forces all data loading onto a single CPU core
questions.explain: pin_memory uses page-locked (non-pageable) host memory, which the CUDA driver can copy to the GPU asynchronously and faster than ordinary pageable memory.

questions.q: Why does reading a dataset split into millions of small files hurt throughput on object storage like S3?
options: Small files compress worse than large files
S3 charges more per request for small objects
Each sample becomes its own request, and per-request latency multiplies across every sample and every rank
S3 has a hard limit on the number of objects per bucket
questions.explain: Object storage has real per-request latency (tens of milliseconds). Millions of tiny files turn that latency into a large cumulative tax; streaming through fewer, larger shards amortizes it.
